quickAnswer: The TV and Gaming Display Capability Checker audits your connected television or monitor for 120Hz refresh rates, HDR color spaces (Display P3 / Rec.2020), and Variable Refresh Rate (VRR) readiness. It features a real-time requestAnimationFrame delta sampler, an HDMI 2.1 bandwidth calculator, a judder and tear simulation pattern, and an optimal TV picture mode calibration checklist for PS5 and Xbox Series consoles. All diagnostics execute locally in your browser.

howTo.name: Audit Refresh Rate and Frame Stability

faq.q: Why is my 120Hz television showing 60Hz in the browser?
faq.a: Several factors can cap browser refresh rates at 60Hz: (1) Windows or macOS display settings may be defaulted to 60Hz; (2) The connected HDMI cable or port may be limited to HDMI 2.0; (3) The television input label may not have 'Enhanced Format' or 'Ultra Deep Color' enabled; (4) The browser hardware acceleration setting may be disabled.

faq.q: What is the difference between HDMI 2.0 and HDMI 2.1?
faq.a: HDMI 2.0 is capped at 18.0 Gbps (TMDS), which permits uncompressed 4K at 60Hz with 8-bit color. HDMI 2.1 expands bandwidth up to 40.0 Gbps (on PS5) and 48.0 Gbps (on Xbox Series X and modern GPUs), enabling uncompressed 4K at 120Hz with 10-bit HDR and Variable Refresh Rate (VRR) simultaneously [Confirmed: HDMI Forum].

faq.q: What is HGiG and why is it recommended over TV Dynamic Tone Mapping?
faq.a: HGiG (HDR Gaming Interest Group) turns off the television's internal dynamic tone mapping algorithm. This allows the console itself to perform tone mapping directly to the display's exact peak luminance clipping point (e.g., 800 nits on OLED). If both the TV Dynamic Tone Mapping and console HDR are enabled, 'double tone mapping' occurs, blowing out specular highlights.

faq.q: Can a web browser directly detect HDMI cable version?
faq.a: No browser has access to low-level physical EDID pin telemetry due to operating system sandbox protections. Instead, this tool measures the delivered software frame timing and CSS display queries while providing a mathematical bandwidth calculator and verification wizard to validate your configuration.

articleHtml:
Television Display Engineering: HDMI 2.1, 120Hz Refresh, and HGiG HDR

Modern televisions have evolved into sophisticated gaming monitors featuring Variable Refresh Rate (VRR), Auto Low Latency Mode (ALLM), and high-frequency 120Hz refresh rates. Maximizing these capabilities requires proper physical cabling and accurate operating system calibration.

HDMI Bandwidth Standards: FRL versus TMDS

Older HDMI 2.0 standards utilize Transition-Minimized Differential Signaling (TMDS) capped at 18.0 Gbps. HDMI 2.1 introduces Fixed Rate Link (FRL), which increases maximum uncompressed bandwidth up to 48.0 Gbps:

$$\text{Throughput (Gbps)} = \frac{\text{Horizontal} \times \text{Vertical} \times \text{Refresh Rate} \times \text{Bits Per Pixel} \times 1.15 \times 1.2}{10^9}$$

A 4K display at 120Hz with 10-bit color in uncompressed RGB (4:4:4) demands approximately 32.1 Gbps of transmission throughput [Confirmed: HDMI Forum]. Consequently, connected PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X systems will automatically fall back to 60Hz or compress color data using 4:2:2 subsampling if connected to an HDMI 2.0 port.

Variable Refresh Rate and Low Framerate Compensation (LFC)

Traditional V-Sync locks frame presentation to the display's fixed refresh cycles (e.g., 16.67ms on 60Hz). When a complex game scene drops from 60 FPS to 52 FPS, V-Sync forces the panel down to 30 FPS, causing severe perceptible judder. Variable Refresh Rate (VRR) synchronizes the television's physical refresh scan directly to the console GPU render completion.

  • PlayStation 5 VRR Range: 48 Hz to 120 Hz via the HDMI 2.1 VRR standard [Confirmed: PlayStation Support].
  • Xbox Series X|S VRR Range: 40 Hz to 120 Hz supporting both HDMI Forum VRR and AMD FreeSync Premium [Confirmed: Xbox Wire].
  • Low Framerate Compensation (LFC): When a game dips below the display's minimum VRR threshold (e.g., below 48 Hz), the display controller multiplies frame delivery (displaying 40 FPS at 80 Hz) to maintain smooth motion without screen tearing.

HDR Tone Mapping: HGiG versus Dynamic Tone Mapping

High Dynamic Range video calibration frequently suffers from double tone mapping. Standard television Dynamic Tone Mapping (DTM) continuously analyzes image histograms on-the-fly, modifying gamma curves and highlight clipping points. In gaming, the console rendering engine already calculates exact scene exposure based on physical camera exposure.

Enabling HGiG (HDR Gaming Interest Group) in TV picture settings disables internal display tone mapping and passes raw highlight values untouched. Calibrating the console's HDR setup screen while in HGiG mode sets the clipping boundary exactly to the panel's physical peak brightness (e.g., 800 nits on standard WOLED, 1,500 nits on QD-OLED or Mini-LED).
